chunks: I lived as a good neighbour to you, and tried my best to look after you from behind, and freed you from the snare of humbleness and the fetters of oppression. This was out of gratitude from me for the little good (from your side), and closing my eyes to what the sight perceived and the body witnessed, of the many misdeeds.

key_terms.إِطْرَاق: Closing the eyes or turning away; ignoring or overlooking.
key_terms.الْمُنْكَر: The misdeeds or faults; that which is disapproved of.
key_terms.جِوَار: Neighbourhood or dwelling together; the state of being a neighbour.
key_terms.حَلَق: A fetter or shackle; a ring or loop used for binding.
key_terms.رَبَق: A snare or noose; a metaphor for a tight constraint or trap.

ai.seo_question: What does it mean to free others from the snare of humiliation according to Shia ethical teachings?
ai.summary: In this passage from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (AS) articulates the principle of *jawar* (good companionship/conduct), demonstrating how a leader or individual can maintain social harmony by actively covering the faults of others (*satr al-ayb*) rather than exposing them. This magnanimity is rooted in the Shia ethical tradition of valuing the minor virtues of others while overlooking their numerous shortcomings, thereby fostering an environment of dignity and reducing social friction.
